subtopics: Why evaluating constructed command strings is dangerous

content.intro: Command injection occurs when data is reinterpreted as shell syntax, often through `eval` or constructed command strings.
content.why_it_matters: Command Injection Risks matters because reliable shell automation depends on making this behavior explicit, testing its boundaries, and documenting environment assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Command injection occurs when untrusted text is treated as shell syntax. Avoid assembling commands into strings and evaluating them with `eval`; validate inputs and pass dynamic values as arguments to a fixed command.

content_blocks.title: How it fits into Bash
content_blocks.text: Command injection occurs when data is reinterpreted as shell syntax, often through `eval` or constructed command strings. Keep the command fixed and pass user-controlled values as quoted data; validate allowed choices rather than trying to escape an arbitrary command.

content_blocks.code:
user_value='hello; not a shell command'
printf '%s\n' "$user_value"

content_blocks.title: Watch out
content_blocks.text: Use arrays and quoted expansions instead of constructing command strings for eval. Practice destructive workflows only in a disposable temporary directory, with preview and confirmation support. Do not assume the same command options or newer Bash features exist on every operating system.

content_blocks.title: Check your result
content_blocks.text: Compare the observed output and exit status with the reference behavior. Change one input at a time, include a boundary or invalid input, and note what differs on your target Bash/utility version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety note
content_blocks.text: Use a local test directory, avoid secrets in commands/history/logs, and check the installed interpreter with `bash --version`. This course remains draft until technical examples and assessments receive subject-matter review.

hints: Reduce the problem to one command or one small function first.
Use quoting and printf to make argument boundaries visible.

content.expected_output: A documented example for “Command Injection Risks” with the observed output/status, one tested boundary case, and an explicit statement of any version or utility dependency.
troubleshooting: If the snippet uses an external command, check availability with `command -v NAME` and consult that program’s local help.
If behavior differs by operating system or Bash version, record `bash --version` and check the official manual linked below.
For syntax-only validation run `bash -n script.sh`; this parses but does not execute the script.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a successful-looking output means the command succeeded.
common_mistakes.why: Output and exit status are separate signals, and a later command may replace `$?`.
common_mistakes.fix: Capture important statuses immediately and check all relevant pipeline stages.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying example commands straight into a production path.
common_mistakes.why: Real paths, permissions, input names, and external utility versions differ.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable fixture and inspect the planned side effects first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating Bash-specific syntax as portable `sh` syntax.
common_mistakes.why: Arrays, `[[ ... ]]`, process substitution, and some parameter operators are extensions.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the interpreter and test the minimum supported version.

summary: Command Injection Risks has specific syntax and behavior; verify it rather than relying on guesswork.
Preserve argument boundaries and keep shell commands separate from untrusted data.
Test successful, boundary, and failure cases in a safe environment.
